blocks.body:
Two people who have never met want to communicate privately over a channel that anyone can read. With classical ciphers they would first need to agree on a secret key, which needs a private channel, which is what they lacked. Public-key cryptography removes the circle: each person publishes an encryption key that anyone may use, and keeps a matching decryption key secret.

RSA, proposed by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman in 1977 (journal version 1978), was the first practical public-key encryption scheme. It needs nothing beyond [[fermat-euler|Euler's theorem]], [[mod-inverse|modular inverses]] and the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]], and its security rests on a single belief: multiplying two large primes is easy, but recovering them from the product is not.

blocks.title: A trapdoor
blocks.body:
A trapdoor function is easy to compute, hard to invert, but easy to invert for someone holding a secret. RSA's function is $m\mapsto m^e\bmod n$. Computing it takes about $2\log_2e$ modular multiplications by repeated squaring. Inverting it means taking $e$-th roots modulo $n$, and nobody knows how to do that efficiently without knowing the factorisation of $n$. With the factorisation, Euler's theorem tells us which power undoes the $e$-th power.

Throughout, $\varphi$ is Euler's function; for distinct primes $p,q$ we have $\varphi(pq)=(p-1)(q-1)$.

blocks.title: The RSA scheme
blocks.body:
Choose distinct primes $p,q$ and put $n=pq$, $\varphi(n)=(p-1)(q-1)$. Choose an exponent $e$ with $\gcd(e,\varphi(n))=1$ and compute

$$d=e^{-1}\bmod\varphi(n),$$

the unique $d$ with $0< d< \varphi(n)$ and $ed\equiv1\pmod{\varphi(n)}$. The public key is $(n,e)$; the private key is $d$ (together with $p$ and $q$). A message is an integer $m$ with $0\le m< n$. Encryption is $c=m^e\bmod n$ and decryption is $m=c^d\bmod n$.

In words: anyone can raise to the $e$-th power modulo $n$; only the holder of $d$ can undo it.

blocks.title: Correctness of RSA
blocks.body:
Let $n=pq$ with $p\ne q$ primes, and let $ed\equiv1\pmod{\varphi(n)}$ with $e,d\ge1$. Then for every integer $m$,

$$m^{ed}\equiv m\pmod n.$$

In particular decryption recovers every message $0\le m< n$, including those not coprime to $n$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Write $ed=1+k(p-1)(q-1)$ with $k\ge0$. We show $m^{ed}\equiv m$ modulo $p$ and modulo $q$.

Modulo $p$: if $p\mid m$, both sides are $0$. Otherwise $m^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p$ by Fermat's little theorem, so

$$m^{ed}=m\cdot\big(m^{p-1}\big)^{k(q-1)}\equiv m\cdot1=m\pmod p.$$

The same argument with the roles of $p$ and $q$ exchanged gives $m^{ed}\equiv m\pmod q$. So $p$ and $q$ both divide $m^{ed}-m$, and since they are distinct primes, $n=pq$ divides it.

blocks.title: Variations and the role of the hypotheses
blocks.body:
The proof only used that $p-1$ and $q-1$ divide $ed-1$. So one may replace $\varphi(n)$ by $\lambda(n)=\operatorname{lcm}(p-1,q-1)$, the Carmichael function, and take $d=e^{-1}\bmod\lambda(n)$, which is often smaller. Both choices decrypt correctly.

The condition that $n$ is squarefree matters. For $n=p^2$ the congruence $m^{ed}\equiv m$ can fail when $p\mid m$: with $n=9$, $\varphi(9)=6$ and $e=d=5$ (since $25\equiv1\pmod6$), the message $m=3$ gives $3^{25}\equiv0\not\equiv3\pmod9$. For $m$ coprime to $n$, Euler's theorem gives $m^{ed}\equiv m$ for any modulus, but RSA needs every message to work.

Decryption can be sped up with the CRT. Precompute $d_p=d\bmod(p-1)$ and $d_q=d\bmod(q-1)$. Then $m_p=c^{d_p}\bmod p$ and $m_q=c^{d_q}\bmod q$ are the residues of $m$ modulo $p$ and $q$ (by Fermat, as in the proof), and $m$ is recovered by combining them. Exponents and moduli are both half the size, which makes decryption about four times faster.

blocks.title: Why breaking RSA seems to require factoring
blocks.body:
If an attacker knows $\varphi(n)$, they can factor $n$: from $\varphi(n)=n-(p+q)+1$ they get $p+q$, and $p,q$ are the roots of $X^2-(p+q)X+n$. Knowing $d$ also allows factoring $n$ by an efficient randomised algorithm, because $ed-1$ is a known multiple of $\lambda(n)$, and that is enough to find a square root of $1$ modulo $n$ other than $\pm1$, as in the Miller–Rabin test of [[primality]]. So recovering the private key is as hard as factoring. Whether decrypting single messages (taking $e$-th roots) is as hard as factoring is not known.

The best classical factoring algorithm for RSA moduli, the general number field sieve, has running time roughly $\exp\big(c(\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}\big)$, which is subexponential but still enormous. One of the largest RSA challenge numbers factored, RSA-250 (829 bits), was finished in 2020 by Boudot, Gaudry, Guillevic, Heninger, Thomé and Zimmermann. Moduli of $2048$ bits are considered safe against classical computers. Shor's quantum algorithm (1994) factors in polynomial time, so a large fault-tolerant quantum computer would break RSA; this is the reason for the current move to post-quantum schemes.

A historical footnote: Clifford Cocks at the British GCHQ found an equivalent scheme in 1973; it was classified and only made public in 1997.

blocks.title: Textbook RSA and real RSA
blocks.body:
The scheme as defined above (textbook RSA) should not be used directly. It is deterministic, so an eavesdropper can test guesses of the message by encrypting them. It is multiplicative: $(m_1m_2)^e=m_1^em_2^e$, so ciphertexts can be combined without decryption. And small messages with small exponent leak: if $m^e< n$, then $c=m^e$ as integers and $m$ is an ordinary $e$-th root. Real systems first pad the message with random bytes in a structured way (for encryption the standard is OAEP).

The same arithmetic gives digital signatures: the owner signs $m$ by computing $s=m^d\bmod n$, and anyone checks $s^e\equiv m\pmod n$. In practice $m$ is a hash of the document, again with padding.

blocks.title: A toy key
blocks.body: Build a toy key with $p=89$, $q=107$, $e=5$. Encrypt $m=1234$ and decrypt it again using the CRT.
blocks.solution:
Here $n=89\cdot107=9523$ and $\varphi(n)=88\cdot106=9328=2^4\cdot11\cdot53$, which is coprime to $5$.

The inverse of $5$ modulo $9328$ comes from the extended Euclidean algorithm:

$$9328=5\cdot1865+3,\qquad5=1\cdot3+2,\qquad3=1\cdot2+1.$$

Back-substituting, $1=3-2=3-(5-3)=2\cdot3-5=2(9328-1865\cdot5)-5=2\cdot9328-3731\cdot5$. So $5^{-1}\equiv-3731\equiv5597\pmod{9328}$, and $d=5597$. Check: $5\cdot5597=27985=3\cdot9328+1$.

Encrypt: $1234^2\equiv8599$, $1234^4\equiv8599^2\equiv6229$, and $1234^5\equiv6229\cdot1234\equiv1525\pmod{9523}$. So $c=1525$.

Decrypt with the CRT: $d_p=5597\bmod88=53$ and $d_q=5597\bmod106=85$. Reduce $c$: $1525\equiv12\pmod{89}$ and $1525\equiv27\pmod{107}$. Then $m_p=12^{53}\bmod89=77$ and $m_q=27^{85}\bmod107=57$. To combine, write $m=57+107t$; we need $57+107t\equiv77\pmod{89}$, i.e. $18t\equiv20\pmod{89}$. Since $18\cdot5=90\equiv1$, $t\equiv100\equiv11$, and $m=57+107\cdot11=1234$.

blocks.title: Knowing phi(n) means knowing p and q
blocks.body: Someone leaks that the toy modulus $n=9523$ has $\varphi(n)=9328$. Factor $n$.

blocks.title: The same message sent three times
blocks.body: Three users have public keys $(n_1,3)$, $(n_2,3)$, $(n_3,3)$ with $n_1=55$, $n_2=391$, $n_3=1189$ (pairwise coprime). The same message $m<55$ is sent to all three, and the ciphertexts are $c_1=3$, $c_2=189$, $c_3=370$. Recover $m$ without factoring anything.
blocks.solution:
Each $c_i\equiv m^3\pmod{n_i}$. By the Chinese remainder theorem there is a unique $C$ modulo $N=n_1n_2n_3=25569445$ with $C\equiv c_i\pmod{n_i}$ for all $i$, and $m^3$ is one such number. Since $m< n_i$ for every $i$, we have $m^3< n_1n_2n_3=N$, so $m^3$ is exactly the representative $C$ in $[0,N)$, not just congruent to it.

Solving the system gives $C=74088$, and the ordinary cube root is $m=42$. Indeed $42^3=74088$, and $74088\bmod55=3$, $74088\bmod391=189$, $74088\bmod1189=370$.

The lesson (due to Håstad in a more general form): with a small exponent, the same unpadded message must never go to several recipients. Padding with fresh randomness for each encryption prevents the attack.

blocks.body:
- $d$ is the inverse of $e$ modulo $\varphi(n)$ (or $\lambda(n)$), not modulo $n$.
- $e$ must be coprime to $\varphi(n)$; otherwise $d$ does not exist and $m\mapsto m^e$ is not injective modulo $n$.
- $p$ and $q$ must be distinct. With $n=p^2$, factoring is a square root, and the correctness theorem fails for multiples of $p$.
- "$m^{ed}\equiv m$ because of Euler's theorem" is only half the argument: Euler's theorem needs $\gcd(m,n)=1$. The CRT proof covers all $m$.
- Choosing $p$ and $q$ very close together lets Fermat's factoring method find them quickly; a very small private exponent $d$ is also dangerous (Wiener's attack).
- Textbook RSA without padding is not secure encryption, even with a huge modulus.

RSA key generation needs fast [[primality]] tests to find the two primes, and the density of primes from the [[pnt|prime number theorem]] tells how many candidates to try. The arithmetic is that of [[fermat-euler]], [[mod-inverse]] (via [[bezout|Bézout]] and the Euclidean algorithm) and the [[crt]]. The other classical public-key idea, key exchange from discrete logarithms, is in [[discrete-log]]; replacing the group of units modulo $p$ by an elliptic curve group ([[elliptic-curves]]) gives shorter keys for the same security. Abstractly, RSA works in the group of units modulo $n$, whose order $\varphi(n)$ is easy to compute only for someone who knows the factorisation; this viewpoint comes from [[groups]] and [[order-primroot]]. The search for faster factoring algorithms draws on [[smooth-powerful|smooth numbers]] and [[sieve-basics|sieve ideas]].

1. With $p=89$, $q=107$, $e=5$, compute $\lambda(n)=\operatorname{lcm}(88,106)$ and the corresponding private exponent $e^{-1}\bmod\lambda(n)$. Check that it decrypts $c=1525$.
2. Show that if two users share the modulus $n$ but use coprime exponents $e_1,e_2$, then anyone who sees $m^{e_1}\bmod n$ and $m^{e_2}\bmod n$ can recover $m$ (assume $\gcd(m,n)=1$).
3. Prove that if two RSA moduli $n_1\ne n_2$ share a prime factor, both can be factored with one gcd computation.
4. Explain why the signature $s=m^d\bmod n$ of $m=m_1m_2\bmod n$ can be computed from the signatures of $m_1$ and $m_2$, and why this means signatures must be computed on padded hashes.
